title: Dynamical Regimes
intro: The same spin-network reservoir behaves very differently depending on whether its Hamiltonian is integrable, ergodic or many-body localised, and only some regimes compute well. This page connects reservoir performance to level statistics and to how fast information spreads, following Martínez-Peña and coauthors (2021).

blocks.text: What you need first

The spin-network reservoir and its parity symmetry from The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir), and the memory capacity of Training, Testing and Measuring Error (#/qrc/start/training-and-testing). From the Quantum Mechanics shelf: eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix and Spin Models (#/quantum/many-body/spin-models) (the XX coupling and the field). Level statistics are explained from scratch below.
What you will be able to do

items: Name the three regimes of a disordered spin network (integrable, ergodic, localised), say what each does to information written on one qubit, and say which parameters produce it.
Compute the probability that an excitation hops between two detuned qubits and use it to explain why strong disorder destroys memory.
Compute the gap ratio from a list of energy levels, state the Poisson and random-matrix values, and explain why symmetry blocks must be separated first.
Read a table of memory capacity against disorder and field and say which regime each row is in.
Apply the rule of thumb for choosing the field, disorder and step length of a spin reservoir.

blocks.text: Why the same model can be great or useless

On The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir) we built a reservoir from fixed random numbers: the couplings $J_{ij}$ and the fields $h_i$. Different draws behave a little differently, as the sweep there showed. But some choices of the numbers are not a little different, they are a different kind of system. Set the field to zero and the model is a set of independent phases; set the disorder large and every qubit sits alone. The same code, the same readout, and the memory goes from 3.3 to nearly 0. This page explains why, using the language of dynamics: how fast does information written on qubit 1 spread through the register, and does it reach independent directions?

A reservoir needs two things from its dynamics. Transport: information must leave the input qubit before the next reset deletes it. Mixing: different past inputs must end up in linearly independent directions of the observable space, so that a linear readout can separate them. The three regimes below differ in which of these they provide.
Three regimes of a disordered spin network
Integrable, or nearly so

Put $h\to0$. Then $H=\sum J_{ij}X_iX_j$, and all the terms commute with one another (every term is a product of $X$s). Commuting terms can be diagonalised together, in the basis of eigenstates of the $X_i$; in that basis the evolution $e^{-iHt}$ is a diagonal matrix of phases. Nothing is scrambled: an operator such as $Z_1(t)$ is a combination of a handful of operators, not an increasingly complicated sum. A large uniform field is also nearly integrable: the field term dominates, the magnetisation $\sum_iZ_i$ is almost conserved, and only the part of the XX terms that conserves it (hopping of an excitation from one qubit to another) acts at leading order; pair creation is detuned by the field. The energy levels of an integrable system have no particular relation to each other (they look like random points on a line: Poisson statistics).
Ergodic (chaotic)

Take $h$ comparable to the coupling scale $J$ and weak disorder. The $Z$ field and the $XX$ coupling do not commute, so the dynamics mixes. Eigenstates look random within each symmetry sector, local information spreads through the register in a few coupling times, and neighbouring energy levels repel each other (Wigner-Dyson statistics; the ensemble is the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble, GOE, because $H$ is a real matrix in the $Z$ basis).
Localised

Make the disorder $W$ much larger than $J$. Neighbouring qubits now have very different field strengths, so their energy levels are detuned and they cannot exchange excitations: this is the same physics as a mismatched pair of pendulums, which cannot pass energy between them. Information written on qubit 1 stays on qubit 1. In a large system (many qubits, strong disorder) this is many-body localisation; in a handful of qubits it is simply strong detuning. Levels are again Poisson.
The detuning formula, worked out

Take two qubits coupled by $JX_1X_2$ with fields $h_1Z_1+h_2Z_2$, and start in $\vert10\rangle$ (qubit 1 excited). $X_1X_2$ connects $\vert10\rangle$ with $\vert01\rangle$ with amplitude $J$; the diagonal energies of those two states are $h_2-h_1$ and $h_1-h_2$. Write $\delta=h_1-h_2$. In the basis $\{\vert01\rangle,\vert10\rangle\}$ the $2\times2$ block has rows $(\delta, J)$ and $(J,-\delta)$ (up to the sign convention for which state gets $+\delta$). Its eigenvalues are $\pm\sqrt{\delta^2+J^2}$, and the standard two-level (Rabi) result is that the largest probability of finding the excitation on qubit 2 is

blocks.caption: Maximum transfer probability for coupling J and detuning delta.

blocks.text: With $\delta=0$ the transfer is complete. With $\delta=J$ it is half. With $\delta=10J$ it is $1\%$. Now compute for the reservoir. In our model each coupling is uniform in $[-0.5,0.5]$ with typical size $\vert J\vert\approx0.25$. The difference of two fields, each uniform in $[-W/2,W/2]$, has typical size $\vert\delta\vert\approx W/3$. Then $P_{\max}=0.0625/(0.0625+\delta^2)$:

items: $W=0$: $\delta=0$, $P_{\max}=1$. Free exchange.
$W=1$: $\delta\approx0.33$, $P_{\max}=0.36$. Partial transfer.
$W=3$: $\delta\approx1$, $P_{\max}=0.059$.
$W=50$: $\delta\approx16.7$, $P_{\max}=2.2\times10^{-4}$. Information essentially never leaves qubit 1.

blocks.text: Be careful what this does and does not say. The formula is for two qubits and a single excitation; the many-qubit reservoir has many paths, and the real picture is a statistical one. But the trend is right and the numbers explain the table below: at $W=50$ the memory is about $0.16$ because qubit 1's information is deleted by the reset before it can move.

Level statistics as a diagnostic
Why we need it

We have a qualitative picture of three regimes. For a real reservoir with 8 or 10 qubits we want a number that says which regime it is in, computed from $H$ alone, without running any task. Level statistics provide one.
The idea in plain words

If a system is integrable or localised, its energy levels are almost independent of each other: two levels can land very close together by chance, as raindrops can land almost on top of each other on a pavement. In a chaotic system all the eigenstates are coupled to all the others, and coupled levels push each other apart: close pairs are rare, as for people who keep a polite distance. Counting how often neighbouring gaps are tiny therefore tells the regime.
The maths
Sort the eigenvalues $E_1\le E_2\le\cdots$ within one symmetry block, take the consecutive gaps $g_k=E_{k+1}-E_k$ and form the ratio of neighbouring gaps

blocks.caption: The gap ratio needs no unfolding of the density of states (Oganesyan and Huse 2007; Atas et al. 2013).

blocks.text: Why a ratio and not the gap? The density of levels varies across the spectrum, so raw gaps have no common scale. In a ratio of two neighbouring gaps the local density cancels. By construction $0\le r\le1$. A worked example with five made-up levels $0,\ 1,\ 3,\ 4.5,\ 5$: the gaps are $1,\ 2,\ 1.5,\ 0.5$ and the ratios are $\min(1,2)/\max(1,2)=0.5$, then $\min(2,1.5)/\max(2,1.5)=0.75$, then $\min(1.5,0.5)/\max(1.5,0.5)=0.333$; the mean is $0.528$ (this is a made-up list, but it happens to look repelled, as GOE does). The Poisson value $2\ln 2-1$ comes from averaging over independent random levels; the GOE number comes from random-matrix theory and numerics.
The symmetry trap, in numbers

The Hamiltonian has the parity symmetry of The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir). Levels from different parity blocks do not repel (they belong to unrelated subspaces), so if you pool the full spectrum you are mixing two independent sets of levels, and the pooled statistics move toward Poisson even for a chaotic system. The program below computes the gap ratio for the weakly disordered reservoir ($h=1$, $W=1$) on the whole spectrum and inside one parity block, for 8 and 10 qubits.

The output: at 8 qubits the whole spectrum gives $0.437$ against $0.528$ in the block; at 10 qubits $0.410$ against $0.550$. The block values are near the GOE value $0.531$ (the 10-qubit value is from only 1 draw and the middle half of $512$ levels, so a few hundredths of scatter is expected); the pooled values sit near but not at Poisson, which would mislead you into calling a chaotic reservoir 'integrable'.

blocks.title: Check yourself: interpreting a gap ratio
blocks.text: A colleague's 10-qubit reservoir gives $\langle r\rangle=0.42$ computed over the full spectrum. Can you conclude it is integrable or localised?
blocks.hint: What did the program show for a reservoir known to be chaotic?
solution: 0.42 is close to the Poisson value 0.386, but the full spectrum mixes the two parity sectors, which never repel each other.
The program gives $0.410$ over the full spectrum for a chaotic 10-qubit reservoir ($h=1$, $W=1$), which is inside the block at $0.55$.
Recompute inside one parity block: near $0.53$ means ergodic; near $0.39$ means integrable or localised, and a small-$h$ or large-$W$ check tells which.

blocks.text: Simulation: regimes against memory
The experiment

The next program connects the diagnostic to performance. For each of five parameter sets it computes the memory capacity of a 4-qubit reservoir (delays 1 to 8, $V=3$, $\Delta t=10$, averaged over three random draws) and the gap ratio of an 8-qubit reservoir with the same $h$ and $W$ (even-parity block, middle half of the spectrum, four draws).

blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Z = np.diag([1, -1]).astype(complex)
def op(o, i, n):
    m = np.array([[1]], complex)
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m
def hamiltonian(n, h, W, rng):
    H = sum(rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) * op(X, i, n) @ op(X, j, n) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n))
    return H + sum((h + rng.uniform(-W / 2, W / 2)) * op(Z, i, n) for i in range(n))

def gap_ratio(n, h, W, reals=10):
    """mean r = min(g_k, g_{k+1}) / max(...) in the even Z-parity sector: Poisson ~0.386, GOE ~0.531"""
    par = np.array([(-1) ** bin(a).count("1") for a in range(2 ** n)])
    rs = []
    for k in range(reals):
        H = np.real(hamiltonian(n, h, W, np.random.default_rng(k)))
        E = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H[np.ix_(par == 1, par == 1)])
        E = E[len(E) // 4: 3 * len(E) // 4]             # middle of the spectrum
        g = np.diff(E); rs += list(np.minimum(g[1:], g[:-1]) / np.maximum(g[1:], g[:-1]))
    return np.mean(rs)

def memory_capacity(n, h, W, seed, dt=10.0, V=3):
    H = hamiltonian(n, h, W, np.random.default_rng(seed)); D = 2 ** n
    E, P = np.linalg.eigh(H); U = P @ np.diag(np.exp(-1j * E * dt / V)) @ P.conj().T
    zd = [np.real(np.diag(op(Z, i, n))) for i in range(n)]
    s = np.random.default_rng(seed + 100).uniform(0, 1, 900); rho = np.eye(D) / D; F = []
    for x in s:
        r4 = rho.reshape(2, D // 2, 2, D // 2); rest = r4[0, :, 0, :] + r4[1, :, 1, :]
        psi = np.array([np.sqrt(1 - x), np.sqrt(x)]); rho = np.kron(np.outer(psi, psi), rest); f = []
        for _ in range(V):
            rho = U @ rho @ U.conj().T; d = np.real(np.diag(rho)); f += [z @ d for z in zd]
        F.append(f)
    F = np.hstack([np.array(F), np.ones((len(s), 1))]); wash, tr = 100, 500; mc = 0
    for d in range(1, 9):
        A = F[wash:wash + tr]; y = s[wash - d:wash + tr - d]
        w = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + 1e-7 * np.eye(A.shape[1]), A.T @ y)
        mc += np.corrcoef(F[wash + tr:] @ w, s[wash + tr - d:len(s) - d])[0, 1] ** 2
    return mc

print("regime                      h      W   MC(4 qubits)  <r>(8 qubits)")
for name, h, W in [("pure XX (commuting)", 0.001, 0), ("clean, h ~ J", 1, 0), ("weak disorder", 1, 1),
                   ("strong disorder", 1, 10), ("very strong disorder", 1, 50)]:
    mc = np.mean([memory_capacity(4, h, W, k) for k in range(3)])
    print(f"{name:24s} {h:6g} {W:4g}   {mc:10.2f}   {gap_ratio(8, h, W, 4):10.3f}")

items: Pure XX ($h=0.001$, $W=0$): $\langle r\rangle=0.395$ (Poisson), MC $2.24$.
Clean, $h=J$-scale ($h=1$, $W=0$): $\langle r\rangle=0.522$ (near GOE), MC $3.30$.
Weak disorder ($W=1$): $\langle r\rangle=0.528$, MC $3.10$.
Strong disorder ($W=10$): $\langle r\rangle=0.408$, MC $1.94$.
Very strong disorder ($W=50$): $\langle r\rangle=0.402$, MC $0.16$.

blocks.text: The two kinds of Poisson regime fail differently. Localisation is catastrophic: written on qubit 1, information never leaves it, and the next reset deletes it, so memory goes to zero ($0.16$ at $W=50$, as the detuning formula predicted: $P_{\max}\approx2\times10^{-4}$). The integrable XX limit keeps some memory ($2.24$), because the XX terms still move information, but without scrambling the features are less independent. The ergodic regime is best ($3.3$ and $3.1$). Note that strong disorder at $W=10$ is already Poisson in the level statistics ($0.408$) while memory is still $1.94$, so the diagnostic and the performance are correlated, not identical.

widget.title: Memory capacity across the field strength

blocks.text: Try this. (1) At $W=1$ the curve is fairly flat around 3.3 across four decades of $h$ (values between about 3.0 and 3.7): four qubits are too few for a sharp transition, and with $\Delta t=10$ even a small field acts over a long time. (2) Raise $W$ to 10: the capacity roughly halves, wandering between 1 and 2.8 for $h\lesssim1$ and falling to about 1 or below for $\log_{10}h\ge0.5$. (3) At $W=30$ it is erratic and mostly below 1 (two isolated points just above), and near zero for $h\gtrsim10$. (4) Back at $W=1$, lower $\Delta t$ to 1: the small-$h$ end weakens (about 2.1 against 3.7), because $h\Delta t$ is too small to break the commuting XX structure within one input period, while the curve peaks near $h\approx1$ at about 4.2.
Why ergodicity helps, and where it stops helping

Ergodic dynamics gives transport and mixing. But fully scrambled dynamics over many qubits drives local observables of most states toward their thermal values, so the differences the readout has to see shrink; in large systems this becomes the concentration problem of Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability). The practical optimum sits in the ergodic regime but near its edge, with enough structure that local features still vary appreciably with the inputs. Martínez-Peña and coauthors, comparing the thermalising and many-body-localised phases of a disordered spin reservoir, found the thermal phase naturally suited to QRC and reported the best performance around the thermalisation transition.

Rule of thumb for spin reservoirs: pick $h\sim J$, disorder $W\lesssim J$, and $J\Delta t$ of a few. Check $\langle r\rangle$ in one symmetry block; if it reads Poisson, the reservoir is either integrable or localised and will waste qubits.

Common mistake: assuming that more disorder is a safe way to 'break symmetry'. Weak disorder is useful (it removes accidental degeneracies, as $W=1$ shows); strong disorder is harmful. The right amount is small compared with the coupling. And do not read a gap ratio from a four-qubit reservoir as precisely as from eight: with 8 levels per parity block the statistics are very rough, and it is better to test performance directly.
Putting it together

Problem. A lab has built a 6-qubit spin reservoir. Couplings are of typical size $0.25$, the field is $h=1$, and a technician reports that the random field offsets have width $W=6$. Memory capacity is disappointing. Diagnose it and suggest a change.

items: Step 1. Compute the typical detuning: $\delta\approx W/3=2$. Then $P_{\max}=0.0625/(0.0625+4)=0.0154$: information barely hops between neighbours.
Step 2. Compare with the table: $W=10$ gave MC $1.94$ and a Poisson gap ratio $0.408$; $W=6$ is between the clean case and that. The problem is detuning, not field strength.
Step 3. Confirm with level statistics: compute $\langle r\rangle$ inside one parity block. If it is near $0.4$ the reservoir is localised; if near $0.53$ the disorder is not the problem.

Step 4. Fix: reduce $W$ to about $1$ ($P_{\max}=0.36$), keep $h\sim J$, and retune $\Delta t$ to a few $1/J$. Re-run the memory test. If MC is still low, look at the readout (shots and features) rather than the dynamics.

blocks.text: The principle: diagnose with a number computed from $H$ alone (transfer probability, gap ratio) before spending hardware time on training.
Key points

items: A reservoir needs transport (information leaves the input qubit before the reset) and mixing (past inputs reach independent features).

Integrable: commuting terms ($h\to0$) or conserved magnetisation (large $h$): no scrambling, Poisson levels. Ergodic: $h\sim J$, weak disorder, random-matrix levels. Localised: $W\gg J$, no transfer, Poisson levels.
Two-qubit transfer: $P_{\max}=J^2/(J^2+\delta^2)$; at $W=50$ it is about $2\times10^{-4}$.
The gap ratio $r=\min(g_k,g_{k+1})/\max(g_k,g_{k+1})$ has mean $2\ln2-1\approx0.386$ for Poisson and about $0.531$ for GOE; compute it within one symmetry block.
The optimum is ergodic but near its edge; very strong scrambling meets the concentration problem.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Name the regime
blocks.text: Three 4-qubit reservoirs with couplings uniform in $[-0.5,0.5]$ are tested. (a) $h=0.001$, $W=0$, block gap ratio of the 8-qubit version $0.40$. (b) $h=1$, $W=0$, gap ratio $0.52$. (c) $h=1$, $W=40$, gap ratio $0.40$. Name the regime of each and rank them by the memory capacity you expect.
blocks.hint: Two of them have Poisson-like statistics for different reasons. Ask in each case whether information can leave qubit 1.
solution: (a) The field is negligible, so all terms are $X_iX_j$ and commute: integrable. Poisson-like ratio. Information still moves (the XX terms are there), but without scrambling.
(b) $h$ comparable to the couplings and no disorder: ergodic. The ratio $0.52$ is close to the GOE value $0.531$.
(c) Typical detuning $W/3\approx13$, so $P_{\max}=0.0625/(0.0625+178)\approx3.5\times10^{-4}$: localised. Information hardly leaves qubit 1 and the reset deletes it.
Ranking (b) $>$ (a) $>$ (c), as in the table on this page: $3.30$, $2.24$, and between $1.94$ ($W=10$) and $0.16$ ($W=50$). The gap ratio alone cannot separate (a) from (c); the parameters can.

blocks.title: Disorder and transfer
blocks.text: With couplings of typical size $\vert J\vert=0.25$ and field offsets uniform in $[-W/2,W/2]$, estimate the typical detuning $\delta$ and the maximal transfer probability between two qubits for $W=2$ and $W=20$.
blocks.hint: The difference of two such offsets has typical size $W/3$; then use $P_{\max}=J^2/(J^2+\delta^2)$.
solution: At $W=2$ exchange is weakened but still happens over several steps; at $W=20$ information essentially stays where it was written, the localised regime.
blocks.answer: About 0.12 for W = 2 and 0.0014 for W = 20

blocks.title: A gap ratio by hand
blocks.text: A block has levels $0,\ 0.5,\ 2.5,\ 3,\ 3.2$. Compute the three ratios $r_k$ and their mean, and say whether the mean is nearer the Poisson or the GOE value (with so few levels, treat the answer as a rough indication only).
solution: Mean $=(0.25+0.25+0.4)/3=0.30$: below the Poisson value $0.386$, so the levels look clustered rather than repelled. Three ratios are far too few to conclude anything.

blocks.title: Why the pooled spectrum misleads
blocks.text: Explain in two or three sentences why pooling the two parity blocks of a chaotic reservoir lowers $\langle r\rangle$, and say by roughly how much for 8 qubits using the program above.
blocks.hint: What do two interleaved independent sequences look like?
solution: Levels in different blocks do not interact, so the pooled list contains two independent sequences interleaved at random; an interleaving makes the pooled levels look like uncorrelated points, which have Poisson statistics, and so close pairs appear that would be forbidden inside one block.
For 8 qubits at $h=1$, $W=1$ the pooled ratio is $0.437$ against $0.528$ inside the even block: a drop of about $0.09$ toward the Poisson $0.386$.
blocks.answer: Independent blocks do not repel; 0.437 against 0.528

blocks.text: Where this is used

The regime diagnostic supports the design rules in Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource), where a reset or damping replaces the disordered Hamiltonian as the source of forgetting, and in the scaling arguments of Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability). For which parameter sets the same model works on hardware, see Analog Platforms (#/qrc/hardware/analog-platforms).
